pack.title: The Cross of the Scriptures: river, king and carved prayer

presentation.era: sixth to early tenth century, with a modern conservation afterlife
presentation.anchor: Clonmacnoise · Flann Sinna · Abbot Colmán · Cross of the Scriptures
presentation.question: How did a river-road settlement turn royal patronage into a carved request that can still be read?
presentation.opening: Six chapters move from the Shannon crossing through the working settlement, king and abbot, carved panels, damaged inscription, and the modern separation of original and replica.
presentation.evidenceLimit: The pack uses geography, surviving buildings and stones, annal notices, official interpretation and the damaged inscription. It does not invent a commissioning scene, a named worker's day, or certainty where panel and inscription readings remain disputed.
presentation.sourceTitle: Cross of the Scriptures, Clonmacnoise settlement evidence and Flann–Colmán records
presentation.sourceDetail: Claims O01–O08 · inscription expansion and panel list remain behind medievalist and art-historian review
presentation.artifactPrompt: Carry the river-road map, three panel readings and the damaged inscription boundary together.
presentation.tegCanDo: Recognise and produce supported Irish for place, work, scale, attention, reading and prayer inside an evidence-led object encounter.

resources.value: O01 · Shannon and east–west route junction
O03 · major ecclesiastical settlement by c. 900
O05 · damaged inscription linking Colmán and Flann
O08 · original indoors and replica outside
Cross of the Scriptures inscription · Henry/Stalley conventional reading with Harbison alternative · specialist packet required

chapters.title: Abhainn is Bóthar · River and road

pages.title: A river running through the middle
pages.body: Clonmacnoise stands beside the abhainn — the River Shannon. In the early medieval world this water was a route rather than a boundary. A bád could carry people, food, stone and news north or south, while a raised east–west bóthar crossed the bog country nearby.
pages.detail: The story begins with movement. River and road explain why people kept arriving at this particular bank.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of the Shannon callows · not documentary evidence

displayItems.detail: People and goods on the Shannon

pages.title: The crossing was the first advantage
pages.body: The river offered transport, fish and access to distant communities. The dry ridges east and west offered another kind of movement. Their meeting made this bank useful before any great stone monument stood here.
pages.detail: A crossroads does not guarantee a town. It creates the conditions in which a religious community, patrons and workers can gather.

pages.title: A community begins here
pages.body: Tradition associates the foundation with Ciarán in the sixth century. The place-name Cluain Mhic Nóis points to a meadow setting; the surviving site shows how a small foundation could become a long-lived ecclesiastical centre. Anseo means here: not a timeless nowhere, but this bank and this crossing.
pages.detail: The foundation story comes through hagiography and later memory. The landscape and archaeology support the place, not every detail of a saint's life.

pages.title: Hear the whole crossing
pages.context: Tá abhainn, bád agus bóthar anseo
pages.body: Listen to river, boat, road and here in one line.

exercise.objective: Recognise the four opening words inside a complete place sentence.
exercise.prompt: Which meaning matches the whole line?
exercise.answer: A river, boat and road are here.

options.text: A river, boat and road are here.

options.rationale: Those words belong to the later monument.
The king has not entered the account yet.

exercise.translation: A river, boat and road are here.

exercise.feedback: The sentence gathers the river, a boat, the road and this place.
exercise.hint: Listen for abhainn, bád, bóthar and anseo.
exercise.recovery: That answer leaves out part of the crossing. Replay the full line.

pages.title: The map was already full of movement
pages.body: People approached this bank from kingdoms, farms, churches and landing places that already had names and obligations. Calling the site remote makes sense only from a modern road map. On its own routes, Clonmacnoise was connected.
pages.detail: The river-road composition must not turn the monastery into a miraculous settlement appearing in empty country.

pages.title: Build the sentence
pages.context: Tá abhainn anseo · A river is here
pages.body: Put the place into one complete Irish line.

exercise.objective: Produce a complete here-sentence with abhainn and anseo.

exercise.translation: A river is here.
exercise.modelText: Tá abhainn anseo.
exercise.feedback: Tá abhainn anseo — the river is placed on this bank.
exercise.hint: Start with Tá, then the thing, then anseo.
exercise.recovery: Keep all three parts in the order Tá · abhainn · anseo.

pages.title: What the place can prove
pages.body: The Shannon, the route lines and the surviving enclosure make the location legible. They do not preserve a sixth-century day as a scene. The app can show why this place worked without inventing a conversation at its foundation.
pages.detail: Place evidence is strong; a detailed founding scene would be reconstruction. The distinction stays inspectable.

pages.title: A crossing can gather a settlement
pages.context: Chapter turn · from route to community
pages.body: The site begins as a precise answer to a practical question: where can people meet? Once a community endures at the crossing, river traffic, burial, patronage and work can reinforce one another. The next chapter follows that growth.
pages.detail: The place changes from a useful bank into a community with enough continuity to leave material traces.

pages.title: Put a boat on the river
pages.context: Tá bád ar an abhainn · A boat is on the river
pages.body: Type the complete line, including the fada.

exercise.objective: Produce a complete sentence using bád and abhainn.
exercise.prompt: Type: A boat is on the river, beside the road.
exercise.answer: Tá bád ar an abhainn, in aice leis an mbóthar.
exercise.translation: A boat is on the river, beside the road.
exercise.modelText: Tá bád ar an abhainn, in aice leis an mbóthar.
exercise.feedback: The boat, river and road now occupy one connected place.
exercise.hint: Bád needs its fada. Add the road with in aice leis an mbóthar.
exercise.recovery: Check the fada in bád and keep leis an mbóthar together.

pages.title: The crossing becomes a working place
pages.context: Clonmacnoise · by the early tenth century
pages.body: Over generations the mainistir became the centre of a much larger baile. Churches and burials sat beside craft, hospitality, farming, movement and obair. Abhainn, bád and bóthar return because the settlement depended on the traffic introduced in the first chapter.
pages.detail: Mainistir names the ecclesiastical centre; baile keeps the wider inhabited settlement in view.

pages.title: Hundreds of names and marks survive
pages.body: Clonmacnoise preserves an exceptional collection of early medieval graveslabs. Many are modest stones rather than royal monuments. Together they keep ordinary belonging visible beside the great crosses and churches.
pages.detail: The learner should meet a populated place, not only a catalogue of famous buildings.

pages.title: A day is made from repeated work
pages.body: A lá — a day — at the settlement required food, repair, writing, teaching, prayer and care for visitors and the dead. Foghlaim means learn. It belongs here because learning depended on people maintaining a place where texts, memory and skilled practice could continue.
pages.detail: No named worker's diary survives for this chapter. The account stays with activities supported by objects, buildings and the settlement's record.

pages.title: Listen, then build the sentence

pages.body: Listen to the whole line, then rebuild it.

exercise.recovery: Keep sa mhainistir with obair and sa bhaile with foghlaim.

pages.title: Learning without a modern campus
pages.body: Later descriptions sometimes call Clonmacnoise a university. That comparison can communicate reach, but it imports a modern institution into an early medieval settlement. What the evidence supports is a major centre of learning, manuscript culture, commemoration and ecclesiastical life.
pages.detail: Use the familiar comparison only as a bridge, never as a literal institutional claim.

pages.title: Notice the place inside the sentence
pages.body: Choose the example that places learning in the settlement.

exercise.objective: Notice how sa places an activity inside a named place.

options.text: Tá mé ag foghlaim sa bhaile.

exercise.translation: I am learning in the settlement.
exercise.modelText: Tá mé ag foghlaim sa bhaile.
exercise.feedback: Tá mé ag foghlaim sa bhaile places the learning in the settlement.
exercise.hint: Look for foghlaim and the place phrase sa bhaile.
exercise.recovery: The other lines name work or a day. Choose the one that contains learning and the settlement.

pages.title: Objects show activity, not a single scripted day
pages.body: Stone, metalwork, buildings, burials and written notices support a complex settlement. They do not let us follow one invented scribe, cook or pilgrim from dawn to dusk. The chapter stays plural: many people, many kinds of work.
pages.detail: This limit removes the inherited fictional scriptorium race while preserving the real human density of the place.

pages.body: Arrange the causal account without inventing a single founding day.

pages.title: A great monument needs a great settlement
pages.context: Chapter turn · from community to patronage
pages.body: By the early tenth century Clonmacnoise could support ambitious building and carving because it was already a network of people, resources and obligations. A king's patronage could now become stone, image and public prayer.
pages.detail: The chapter moves from daily continuity to the political scale of Flann Sinna and Abbot Colmán.

pages.title: Bring the crossing back
pages.context: Tá baile anseo, idir abhainn agus bóthar
pages.body: Retrieve the place logic after learning about the settlement.

exercise.objective: Reuse the route and place words in a complete line.
exercise.prompt: Type: A settlement is here, between river and road.
exercise.answer: Tá baile agus mainistir anseo; tá obair agus foghlaim ann gach lá.
exercise.translation: A settlement and monastery are here; work and learning happen there every day.
exercise.modelText: Tá baile agus mainistir anseo; tá obair agus foghlaim ann gach lá.
exercise.feedback: The complete sentence retrieves the inhabited and ecclesiastical place together.
exercise.hint: Name baile and mainistir first; work and learning follow.
exercise.recovery: Keep obair agus foghlaim together before ann gach lá.

chapters.title: Rí agus Ab · King and abbot

pages.title: A king enters the stone record
pages.body: Flann Sinna was a rí whose power depended on alliances, rivals and visible patronage. The mainistir, baile, obair and foghlaim of Clonmacnoise made royal attention useful; royal support made large work possible.
pages.detail: Rí is introduced through a named person, not as a generic medieval title.

displayItems.title: Flann Sinna
displayItems.detail: A powerful king seeking durable patronage

pages.title: The annals record another shared work
pages.body: The annals associate Flann Sinna and Abbot Colmán with the building of the great church at Clonmacnoise in 909. That notice belongs beside the cross, not inside its damaged lettering. Together they show a relationship expressed through building and memory.
pages.detail: The church notice and cross inscription are two pieces of evidence. They must not be collapsed into one quotation.

pages.title: Making turns authority into a public object
pages.body: Déan means make or do. A cros this mór — big — required planning, skilled labour and material. Its small details, beag by comparison, still mattered because hands, faces, clothes and gestures carried the stories a viewer was meant to recognise.
pages.detail: Scale works in two directions: the cross commands attention from a distance, while its panels reward close looking.

displayItems.title: beag
displayItems.detail: The carved detail seen up close

displayItems.title: déan
displayItems.detail: The labour that joins both scales

pages.title: Say role, action and scale
pages.context: Déan cros mhór don rí le sonraí beaga
pages.body: Record the model, then compare without a score.

exercise.objective: Hear and produce rí, déan, cros, mór and beag in a complete instruction.
exercise.prompt: Record: Déan cros mhór don rí le sonraí beaga.
exercise.answer: Déan cros mhór don rí le sonraí beaga.

exercise.modelText: Déan cros mhór don rí le sonraí beaga.
exercise.feedback: The line joins patron, making, monumental scale and close detail.
exercise.hint: Keep rí long and clear; beaga closes the line.
exercise.recovery: If recording is unavailable, listen once more and continue with the model line.

pages.title: Patronage is a relationship, not a work order
pages.body: The surviving sources connect Flann, Colmán and the monument, but they do not preserve a meeting in which the king dictates a panel programme. The cross emerged from a community of carvers, patrons and interpreters whose exact negotiations are lost.
pages.detail: The story can make patronage legible without inventing a commission scene.

pages.title: The patron's name enters a repeated public act
pages.body: A monument can magnify a king without becoming a secular advertisement. The prayer request places Flann's name inside worship and memory, while the scale and position of the cross make that relationship publicly visible.
pages.detail: Political and devotional meanings reinforce one another here; the account should not force the cross into only one category.

pages.title: Complete the making line
pages.context: Déan cros mhór · Make a big cross
pages.body: Choose the word that turns material into action.

exercise.objective: Use déan in a complete imperative phrase.
exercise.prompt: Complete: ___ cros mhór.
exercise.answer: Déan
exercise.translation: Make a big cross.
exercise.modelText: Déan cros mhór.
exercise.feedback: Déan cros mhór — make a big cross.
exercise.hint: Choose the verb meaning make or do.
exercise.recovery: Mór describes scale and rí names the patron. The missing word is the action.

pages.title: Two records, one careful relationship
pages.body: The annal notice supports Flann and Colmán building together at the church. The cross inscription, in its conventional reading, links Colmán, the making of the cross and King Flann. Exact letters and grammar remain a specialist question for the next chapter.
pages.detail: The relationship is the learner-facing claim; the disputed expansion stays available in the evidence detail.

pages.body: Keep the four jobs distinct.

exercise.answer: all pairs
exercise.feedback: King, make, big and small now describe different parts of the commission.
exercise.hint: Rí is a person; déan is an action.
exercise.recovery: Those two roles do not match. Try the remaining meaning.

pages.title: Read what the evidence links
pages.body: Choose the claim held by both the wider record and the conventional inscription reading.

exercise.objective: Identify the supported relationship among Flann, Colmán and monumental work.
exercise.prompt: What is the secure chapter-level claim?
exercise.answer: Flann and Colmán are connected to major building and the cross.

exercise.hint: Choose the relationship that does not require invented dialogue.
exercise.recovery: The sources do not preserve a design meeting or a single named carver.

pages.title: The commission becomes a public question
pages.context: Chapter turn · from patronage to object
pages.body: The king and abbot now recede behind the thing they helped bring into being. The next task is physical: stand before the surviving cross, move from its large silhouette to its small panels, and ask how stone was made to speak.
pages.detail: Authority has become an object that later viewers can still inspect and challenge.

pages.title: Build the sentence
pages.body: Use a complete sentence without inventing the design meeting.

exercise.translation: Colmán makes a big cross for the king, with small details.

exercise.feedback: The line carries the conventional relationship while practising large form and small detail.
exercise.hint: Begin with Déanann Colmán; le sonraí beaga closes the line.
exercise.recovery: Keep don rí before the detail phrase.

chapters.title: An Chros Chloiche · The stone cross

pages.title: Stone becomes a reading surface
pages.context: Cross of the Scriptures · early tenth century
pages.body: The cros returns, now as a form carved in cloch. The rí, the action déan and the mór/beag change of scale remain inside the object. Seas means stand; féach means look. The learner moves from the large ringed form to small scriptural scenes.
pages.detail: This chapter treats the cross as an object with scale, surface and a required way of looking.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of carved sandstone relief · not documentary evidence

displayItems.title: cloch
displayItems.detail: The material that carries the carving

displayItems.title: féach
displayItems.detail: The close attention the panels need

pages.title: Two crosses occupy the modern site
pages.body: The original high cross is protected indoors. A replica stands outside in the historical enclosure. A visitor can therefore meet the form in its landscape and the worn carving under shelter, but those encounters belong to two different objects.
pages.detail: The interface must always say which object is being shown. Replica is not a lesser truth; it is a different evidential role.

pages.title: Images organise the shaft
pages.body: The surviving carving is arranged in panels. Official interpretation identifies scenes including the Crucifixion, the Last Judgement and Christ in the Tomb. Their order and exact reading are art-historical work, not a picture-book certainty.
pages.detail: The learner can recognise named scenes while keeping room for specialist correction of individual figures and sequences.

displayItems.title: Christ in the Tomb
displayItems.detail: A scene read through worn carving

pages.title: Hear the instruction at the object
pages.context: Seas anseo agus féach ar an gcros chloiche
pages.body: Listen to a complete instruction before choosing its meaning.

exercise.recovery: The phrase asks you to stand and look, not to pray yet.

pages.title: The bare stone may not be the whole appearance
pages.body: Experts have suggested that high crosses were originally painted. Weathering leaves the modern viewer with carved form and traces rather than the full early medieval visual field. The app must not colour the object as if a particular scheme were known.
pages.detail: Potential colour is a bounded interpretive note, not licence for decorative reconstruction.

pages.title: Type the viewing instruction
pages.body: Use both attention verbs in one short line.

exercise.objective: Produce a complete instruction using seas, anseo and féach.
exercise.prompt: Type: Stand here and look.
exercise.answer: Seas anseo agus féach ar an gcros chloiche.
exercise.translation: Stand here and look at the stone cross.
exercise.modelText: Seas anseo agus féach ar an gcros chloiche.
exercise.feedback: Position, attention, object and material now sit in one instruction.
exercise.hint: Begin with Seas anseo; ar an gcros chloiche completes the line.
exercise.recovery: Check that anseo comes before agus féach.

pages.title: A panel can be visible and still uncertain
pages.body: A worn figure, gesture or object may support more than one identification. For the learning path, the named major scenes remain provisional until the art-historian review closes. The image itself should stay available beside the interpretation.
pages.detail: Seeing and naming are separate acts. The interface must let the learner inspect what prompted the label.

pages.context: Stand · see the form · inspect a panel · read the limit

exercise.modelText: Stand before the cross → see the whole form → inspect a panel → read its evidence note

pages.title: Answer what you see
pages.context: Cad a fheiceann tú? · What do you see?
pages.body: Choose the answer that names the material object.

exercise.feedback: Feicim cros chloiche — I see a stone cross.
exercise.hint: Choose the answer with both the object and its material.
exercise.recovery: The other answers name only a route or a person.

pages.title: The image leads down to letters
pages.context: Chapter turn · from panel to inscription
pages.body: Looking establishes what the cross asks of the body: stand, move closer, compare. The surviving letters ask for another kind of attention. They are damaged, distributed around the base and entangled with competing scholarly readings.
pages.detail: The next chapter moves from seeing figures to reading an incomplete text.

pages.title: Bring the full object back
pages.body: Retrieve material, scale and place in one sentence.

exercise.objective: Reuse cros, mór, cloch and anseo after the panel encounter.
exercise.prompt: Type: A big stone cross is here.
exercise.answer: Tá cros mhór chloiche anseo.
exercise.translation: A big stone cross is here.
exercise.modelText: Tá cros mhór chloiche anseo.
exercise.feedback: The sentence carries the whole monument before the next close reading.
exercise.hint: Begin Tá cros, then describe it before adding anseo.
exercise.recovery: Keep mhór chloiche together between cros and anseo.

pages.title: Damaged letters still ask for action
pages.body: Seas and féach brought the learner to the cros chloiche. Léigh now means read; guí means pray. The conventional reading connects Colmán with making the cross for King Flann and includes a prayer for Flann. Reading it anois means following visible letters and scholarly reconstruction.
pages.detail: The Irish is useful because the object's surviving text is itself an instruction to remember and pray.

pages.title: The text runs across more than one face
pages.body: Published readings join fragments from the cross's faces. One portion asks for a prayer for Flann; another associates Colmán, the making of the cross and King Flann. Gaps and worn letters make punctuation and expansion part of the interpretation.
pages.detail: A clean modern sentence is an editorial bridge. It must never masquerade as an undamaged line visible on the stone.

displayItems.title: Gaps
displayItems.detail: Letters and grammar reconstructed by editors

pages.title: A king's name enters communal memory
pages.body: A request for prayer makes the viewer part of a continuing act of memory. It does not simply label the donor. The inscription places royal patronage inside a religious practice that outlasts the king's life.
pages.detail: The cross is political and devotional at once; neither register cancels the other.

displayItems.title: Memory
displayItems.detail: A name carried beyond a reign

pages.title: Listen, then build the sentence
pages.context: Léigh an t-inscríbhinn anois agus guí
pages.body: Listen, then rebuild the complete instruction.

exercise.prompt: Listen, then put the words in order.
exercise.answer: Léigh an t-inscríbhinn anois agus guí.
exercise.translation: Read the inscription now and pray.

pages.title: Scholars disagree at the damaged edge
pages.body: Different scholars have proposed different expansions and relationships among the words. The current draft follows the reading supported by Françoise Henry and Roger Stalley, while keeping Peter Harbison's alternative in the specialist packet.
pages.detail: This is not a dispute to flatten into a quiz answer. The art-historian and inscription review must choose the learner-facing wording.

pages.title: A transcription is a viewing tool
pages.context: Stone surface · drawn letters · editorial choices
pages.body: A diplomatic transcription can preserve gaps, uncertain letters and line breaks that a smooth translation hides. Placed beside the cross, it helps the learner return from modern type to the damaged surface instead of replacing the stone with a clean sentence.
pages.detail: The final inscription view needs both the object and a review-approved transcription; neither is sufficient alone.

pages.title: Tap the matching pairs
pages.body: Keep reading, praying and present time distinct.

exercise.objective: Connect the final chapter words to their meanings.
exercise.prompt: Match each Irish word to its meaning.
exercise.answer: all pairs
exercise.feedback: Read, pray, now: three words that describe the modern encounter.
exercise.hint: Léigh acts on text; guí is the devotional action.
exercise.recovery: Those do not match. Try the remaining meaning.

pages.title: Translation is an argument with the surface
pages.body: The cross supports the presence of Flann's name, prayer language and a making relationship involving Colmán. A fully punctuated English translation depends on editorial choices. The app therefore shows a bounded paraphrase first and the transcription history on request.
pages.detail: The exact letter-by-letter reading remains an open specialist gate in this draft.

pages.title: Complete the present encounter
pages.body: Choose the time word that brings the old inscription into the present.

exercise.objective: Use anois in a complete instruction.
exercise.prompt: Complete: Léigh ___.
exercise.answer: anois
exercise.translation: Read now.
exercise.modelText: Léigh anois.
exercise.feedback: Léigh anois — read now.
exercise.hint: Choose the word meaning now.
exercise.recovery: The missing word is time, not an object or person.

pages.title: Choose the honest inscription claim
pages.body: Apply the evidence boundary before the county closes.

exercise.objective: Distinguish a bounded conventional reading from false certainty.
exercise.prompt: Which statement fits the surviving inscription?
exercise.answer: It links prayer, Flann, Colmán and the making of the cross, but damaged letters affect the exact reading.

options.text: It links prayer, Flann, Colmán and the making of the cross, but damaged letters affect the exact reading.
options.rationale: This preserves the evidence and limit.

options.text: Every letter survives clearly and scholars agree on one translation.
options.rationale: The inscription is damaged and debated.

options.text: It records Flann's spoken instructions to the carvers.

exercise.feedback: The relationship is readable; the exact expansion remains specialist work.
exercise.hint: Choose the answer that keeps both meaning and damage visible.
exercise.recovery: A perfect transcript or a recorded speech would exceed the evidence.

pages.title: The reading changes how the cross is carried
pages.context: Chapter turn · object, request and memory
pages.body: The cross is no longer only a large carved object. It is a damaged text that names power, asks for prayer and reveals the labour of later editors. The final chapter follows what happened when preservation separated the original from its outdoor place.
pages.detail: The learner leaves with a method: inspect the object, read the claim and keep the damaged edge visible.

pages.title: Carry the request in Irish
pages.context: Guí ar son Flann · Pray for Flann
pages.body: Type the short line the inscription's conventional reading makes meaningful.

exercise.objective: Produce guí in a phrase linked to the named king.
exercise.prompt: Type: Pray for Flann.
exercise.answer: Léigh anois agus guí ar son Flann.
exercise.translation: Read now and pray for Flann.
exercise.modelText: Léigh anois agus guí ar son Flann.
exercise.feedback: The line carries reading, present time and prayer for the named king.
exercise.hint: Begin Léigh anois; guí carries a fada.
exercise.recovery: Keep ar son Flann together at the end.

chapters.title: Bunaidh agus Macasamhail · Original and replica

pages.title: The original now stands under shelter
pages.body: The original cross is indoors anois; the outdoor figure is a replica. The move protects the carved cloch and inscription from further exposure. The actions léigh and guí still belong to the encounter, but the relationship among object, sky, churches and river has changed.
pages.detail: Preservation solves one problem by creating another kind of distance.

pages.title: 1991 marks a change in the encounter
pages.body: The original high crosses were moved into the visitor centre in 1991 and replicas placed outside. That date belongs to the object's modern biography. It should not be hidden behind an image that makes every view look ancient and uninterrupted.
pages.detail: Conservation history is part of provenance, not administrative trivia.

pages.title: The cross belongs to a larger surviving field
pages.body: The cross gains meaning from the settlement around it: churches, round towers, hundreds of graveslabs and the Shannon bank. Returning to the whole place prevents one royal monument from swallowing the lives that made and used the community.
pages.detail: The closing composition widens from inscription detail back to the inhabited crossroads.

displayItems.title: River
displayItems.detail: The route that keeps the place connected

pages.title: Notice here and now
pages.body: Choose the sentence that places the protected original in the present.

exercise.objective: Distinguish place from present time in a complete sentence.
exercise.prompt: Which line means: The original cross is here now?
exercise.answer: Tá an chros bhunaidh anseo anois.

options.text: Tá an chros bhunaidh anseo anois.

options.rationale: This says here but not now.
This does not give the place clearly.

exercise.translation: The original cross is here now.
exercise.modelText: Tá an chros bhunaidh anseo anois.
exercise.feedback: Anseo locates the cross; anois locates the encounter in time.
exercise.hint: Look for both anseo and anois.
exercise.recovery: One word answers where; the other answers when. Choose the line with both.

pages.title: A protected object is not a finished argument
pages.body: Moving the cross indoors slows weathering; it does not close debate about its panels or inscription. New imaging, comparison and scholarship can change how worn details are read. The public account should name its review scope and revision.
pages.detail: The draft remains behind the medieval art, inscription and rights gates recorded in its source brief.

pages.title: Speak the present encounter
pages.context: Tá an chloch agus an chros anseo anois
pages.body: Record and compare the line without a pronunciation score.

exercise.objective: Produce cloch, cros, anseo and anois in a complete sentence.
exercise.prompt: Record: Tá an chloch agus an chros anseo anois.
exercise.answer: Tá an chloch agus an chros anseo anois.
exercise.translation: The stone and the cross are here now.
exercise.audioText: Tá an chloch agus an chros anseo anois.
exercise.modelText: Tá an chloch agus an chros anseo anois.
exercise.feedback: You carried material, object, place and time in one line.
exercise.hint: Keep anseo and anois distinct at the end.
exercise.recovery: If recording is unavailable, replay the model and continue without saving audio.

pages.title: What this county account can claim
pages.body: The account can show why the site mattered, how a large settlement supported monumental work, how Flann and Colmán enter the record, what survives on the cross and where interpretation remains contested. It cannot recover a private commissioning scene or an uncontested perfect inscription.
pages.detail: The closing evidence page gathers the county's claims without flattening their different certainties.

pages.title: Put them in order
pages.context: Outdoor original · conservation move · indoor original · outdoor replica
pages.body: Sequence preservation without confusing the two objects.

exercise.objective: Reconstruct the original-and-replica change.
exercise.prompt: Put them in the right order.
exercise.answer: Original outdoors → conservation move → original indoors → replica outdoors
exercise.translation: Original outdoors; move; original indoors; replica outdoors.
exercise.modelText: Original outdoors → conservation move → original indoors → replica outdoors
exercise.feedback: The protected original and outdoor replica now occupy different parts of the encounter.
exercise.hint: The original must move before the replica can take its outdoor place.
exercise.recovery: Do not put the replica before the conservation move.

pages.title: Choose the complete county claim
pages.body: Distinguish the supported story from the attractive invented one.

exercise.objective: Identify the county account that keeps its evidence limits.
exercise.prompt: Which summary can this pack support?
exercise.answer: A river-road settlement, royal patronage and a surviving cross can be followed, while panel and inscription readings retain open limits.

options.text: A river-road settlement, royal patronage and a surviving cross can be followed, while panel and inscription readings retain open limits.
options.rationale: This is the pack's evidence-grounded account.

options.text: A named scribe records every event in a diary.
options.rationale: No such diary anchors the story.

options.text: Every panel and letter has one uncontested reading.

exercise.feedback: The complete account joins place, people, object and uncertainty.
exercise.hint: Choose the account that includes both what survives and what remains open.
exercise.recovery: The other answers invent a founding scene or claim perfect certainty.

pages.title: Carry a method, not a trophy
pages.body: Offaly closes with a practice of attention: follow the route, see the settlement, stand before the object, read the letters and keep the damaged edge. The cross enters the collection as surviving evidence; the twenty words enter review only after Learning mode is complete.
pages.detail: Story completion can open the next county without claiming that its language has been learned.

pages.title: Bring the request back one last time
pages.context: Léigh an chloch anois agus guí
pages.body: Retrieve reading, stone, time and prayer after the full account.

exercise.objective: Produce a closing sentence that reuses the inscription language.
exercise.prompt: Type: Read the stone now and pray.
exercise.answer: Léigh an chloch anois agus guí.
exercise.translation: Read the stone now and pray.
exercise.modelText: Léigh an chloch anois agus guí.
exercise.feedback: The closing line carries object, action and present encounter together.
exercise.hint: Begin Léigh an chloch; anois agus guí completes the line.
exercise.recovery: Check the order: object before time, prayer at the end.
